title: Photographing near a poker game in a neighborhood bar
summary: A habitue wanted him to fake a flash photo of a card game during a newspaper gambling exposé; he declined. Gambling was ubiquitous and public gambling houses ran wide open.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: New Orleans Item was doing an expose on gambling, and there was a poker game going on in the back room of the place. And one of the habitués spotted my camera in flash and had this great plan that would give everybody a laugh where I would go in and take a flash picture or perhaps just pretend to take a flash picture of the card game, and I managed in a fairly friendly manner to decline, but I got nervous every time I walked by the card room to go to the John after that.
Facing the band, the John was to the left.
Yeah, they had the entrance right there.
Anyway, was there much gambling going on in the dance halls? I'm trying to think of some that I noticed.
This wasn't a dance hall, actually. It was a neighborhood bar, and I don't really, if there was room for dancing, it was minimal.

But the band was there, so I suspect there was a little bit, but it wasn't a terribly big place. I didn't, in the neighborhood places, I didn't see much gambling, but I suspect there may have been some if people felt like it. Gambling, private games at any rate, were pretty ubiquitous, certainly at the time. There was a lot of public gambling going on, too. I was never quite sure why the item was so busy with it, because both the gambling houses in Jefferson and St. Bernard Parish were running wide open at the time, and did for some years thereafter.
